All topics · Statistics · Lesson 14 · C&B §2.2

Expected values

Two blocks, about 20 minutes of reading and 35 of lesson. One win: find the average of g(X) without first finding the distribution of g(X), and prove that the mean is the best constant guess under squared error.

Why this lesson

The last two lessons found the pdf of \(Y = g(X)\). Often that's more than you need. If all you want is the average of \(Y\), say the mean squared error of a prediction or the average log of a ratio, there's a shortcut: average \(g(x)\) directly against the distribution of \(X\) you already have. This section of the book states that shortcut as the definition of \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\). It also shows that some averages don't exist, and proves the fact behind every squared-error loss you've trained a model on: the best constant guess for \(X\) is its mean.

Formula boxes take expressions: * for ×, /, ^ for powers, exp( ), log( ) (natural log), sqrt( ). After each right answer, say honestly whether you knew it or guessed.

Warm-up: one more look at the monotone formula (about 5 minutes)

From lessons 12 and 13. Last time, one question came out with the right shape but a coefficient of \(\tfrac13\) where \(3\) belonged. The formula's derivative factor is where that slip lives, and one check catches it every time.

Recap: the monotone formula, and the check

If \(g\) is monotone on the support of \(X\), then on the support of \(Y = g(X)\)

$$ f_Y(y) = f_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\Bigl\lvert \tfrac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y) \Bigr\rvert. $$

The factor is the derivative of the inverse, taken with respect to \(y\). The check: a pdf integrates to 1. If your \(f_Y\) integrates to anything else, the derivative factor (or the support) is wrong.

\(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) and \(Y = -\tfrac13\log X\). Someone gives \(f_Y(y) = \tfrac13 e^{-3y}\) for \(y > 0\). Apply the check: compute \(\int_0^\infty \tfrac13 e^{-3y}\,dy\). (A fraction or a decimal to 4 places.)

\(\int_0^\infty \tfrac13 e^{-3y}\,dy = \tfrac13\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac19\). Not 1, so the proposed \(f_Y\) is wrong, off by a factor of 9. The right factor: \(g^{-1}(y) = e^{-3y}\) and \(\bigl\lvert\frac{d}{dy}e^{-3y}\bigr\rvert = 3e^{-3y}\) [chain rule], so \(f_Y(y) = 3e^{-3y}\), which integrates to 1. A likely cause of the \(\tfrac13\): dividing by the inner derivative \(-3\) instead of multiplying by it.

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Example 2.1.4, numbers changed. \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) and \(Y = -\tfrac12\log X\). Find \(f_Y(y)\) for \(y > 0\), check that it integrates to 1, then give \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac14\right)\). (An expression with exp( ), or a decimal to 4 places.)

\(g^{-1}(y) = e^{-2y}\), \(\bigl\lvert\frac{d}{dy}e^{-2y}\bigr\rvert = 2e^{-2y}\), \(f_X = 1\), so \(f_Y(y) = 2e^{-2y}\) (exponential with rate 2). Check: \(\int_0^\infty 2e^{-2y}\,dy = 1\). At \(y = \tfrac14\): \(2e^{-1/2} \approx 1.2131\).

\(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) and \(Y = -\tfrac12\log X\). Which step is wrong?

  1. \(-\tfrac12\log x\) is decreasing on \((0, 1)\), so the monotone formula applies.
  2. Solving \(y = -\tfrac12\log x\) gives \(g^{-1}(y) = e^{-2y}\), and \(Y\) takes values in \((0, \infty)\).
  3. The derivative factor is \(\bigl\lvert g'(x)\bigr\rvert = \tfrac{1}{2x}\), which at \(x = e^{-2y}\) gives \(\tfrac12 e^{2y}\).
  4. So \(f_Y(y) = 1\cdot\tfrac12 e^{2y}\) for \(y > 0\).

The formula multiplies by the derivative of the inverse, \(\bigl\lvert\frac{d}{dy}e^{-2y}\bigr\rvert = 2e^{-2y}\), which is the reciprocal of \(\lvert g'(x)\rvert\) at \(x = g^{-1}(y)\). The check exposes it at once: \(\tfrac12 e^{2y}\) grows without bound, so its integral over \((0, \infty)\) is infinite, not 1.

Block 1: read first (about 20 minutes)

Reading

Casella & Berger, Statistical Inference, 2nd ed., §2.2 "Expected Values", pp. 55–59: from the section heading on p. 55 to the end of Example 2.2.7, just before §2.3. About four and a half pages.

Read closely: Definition 2.2.1 (p. 55); Example 2.2.2, the exponential mean (pp. 55–56); Example 2.2.4, the Cauchy mean (pp. 56–57); Theorem 2.2.5 (p. 57); Example 2.2.6, minimizing distance (p. 58); equations (2.2.4)–(2.2.5) and Example 2.2.7 (pp. 58–59). Skim: Example 2.2.3, the binomial mean (p. 56). It's a counting identity; the lesson has it in a box if you want it.

Notation traps:

  • C&B's exponential(\(\lambda\)) has mean \(\lambda\): \(f(x) = \tfrac1\lambda e^{-x/\lambda}\). Many other books, and most software, write \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) with mean \(1/\lambda\). Check which one a problem means before you use "the mean is \(\lambda\)".
  • \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\) means \(\mathrm E[g(X)]\), not \((\mathrm E\,g)(X)\), and \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2\) means \(\mathrm E[(X - b)^2]\).
  • The aside after Definition 2.2.1: C&B note that Ross (1988) calls this the "law of the unconscious statistician", and say they don't find it amusing. Because C&B take the formula as the definition of \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\), it needs no proof here (my comment, not theirs); Exercise 2.21 proves that it agrees with computing \(\mathrm E Y\) from \(f_Y\) when \(g\) is monotone.
  • In Example 2.2.6, "add \(\pm\mathrm E X\)" means add and subtract it.

C&B give two ways to compute \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\), equations (2.2.4) and (2.2.5). What does each one need you to know, and which did Example 2.2.7 use?

(2.2.4) needs only f_X: integrate g(x) f_X(x). (2.2.5) needs the pdf of Y = g(X) first, then integrate y f_Y(y). Example 2.2.7 does both for E(−log X) with X uniform(0, 1) and gets 1 each way. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

What does Definition 2.2.1 require for \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\) to exist, and how does Example 2.2.4 show the Cauchy has no mean?

E|g(X)| must be finite. For the Cauchy, E|X| = (2/π)∫₀^∞ x/(1+x²) dx = lim (1/π) log(1+M²) = ∞. Reading note, not graded for mastery.

What surprised or confused you in the reading? (Optional.)

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

1. An average weighted by probability (from the reading, about 7 minutes)

Start with something you can count. Roll a fair die; \(X\) is the face. Each face has probability \(\tfrac16\), so the probability-weighted average is

$$ \mathrm E X = \sum_{x=1}^{6} x\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac{21}{6} = 3.5 . $$

Not a value \(X\) can take, and it doesn't need to be: it's the long-run average of many rolls.

Now average a function of \(X\). What's the average of \(X^2\)? \(X^2\) takes the values \(1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36\), each with probability \(\tfrac16\), because each comes from exactly one face. So

$$ \mathrm E X^2 = \sum_{x=1}^{6} x^2\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac{91}{6} \approx 15.17 . $$

You never wrote down the pmf of \(Y = X^2\) as a separate table. You weighted \(g(x) = x^2\) by \(P(X = x)\).

Name it (Definition 2.2.1). For any function \(g\),

$$ \mathrm E\,g(X) = \begin{cases} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f_X(x)\,dx & X \text{ continuous} \\ \sum_x g(x) P(X = x) & X \text{ discrete,} \end{cases} $$

provided \(\mathrm E\lvert g(X)\rvert < \infty\). With \(g(x) = x\) this is the mean, \(\mathrm E X\). Continuous: replace "probability of each value" by "density times \(dx\)".

Example 2.2.2, every line. \(X\) is exponential with mean \(\lambda\): \(f_X(x) = \tfrac1\lambda e^{-x/\lambda}\) for \(x \ge 0\).

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm E X &= \int_0^\infty x\,\tfrac1\lambda e^{-x/\lambda}\,dx && \text{[definition; } f_X = 0 \text{ for } x < 0\text{]}\\ &= \Bigl[-x e^{-x/\lambda}\Bigr]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-x/\lambda}\,dx && \text{[by parts: } u = x,\ dv = \tfrac1\lambda e^{-x/\lambda}dx,\ v = -e^{-x/\lambda}\text{]}\\ &= 0 + \int_0^\infty e^{-x/\lambda}\,dx && \text{[}x e^{-x/\lambda} \to 0 \text{ as } x \to \infty\text{; it is 0 at } x = 0\text{]}\\ &= \lambda && \text{[}\textstyle\int_0^\infty e^{-x/\lambda}dx = \Bigl[-\lambda e^{-x/\lambda}\Bigr]_0^\infty\text{]} \end{aligned} $$

Why the parameter is called the mean. In C&B's parametrization \(\lambda\) is \(\mathrm E X\). With the rate form \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), the same calculation gives \(1/\lambda\).

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.17(a). \(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 3x^2\) for \(0 < x < 1\). What is \(\mathrm E X\)? (A fraction or a decimal to 3 places.)

\(\mathrm E X = \int_0^1 x\cdot 3x^2\,dx = \int_0^1 3x^3\,dx = \tfrac34 = 0.75\). The mass piles up near 1, so the mean sits right of \(\tfrac12\).

\(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 2e^{-2x}\) for \(x \ge 0\). What is \(\mathrm E X\)? (A fraction or a decimal to 3 places.)

This is C&B's exponential with \(\lambda = \tfrac12\) (\(\tfrac1\lambda = 2\) and \(e^{-x/\lambda} = e^{-2x}\)), so \(\mathrm E X = \tfrac12\). Directly: \(\int_0^\infty 2x e^{-2x}\,dx = \tfrac12\). In rate form, rate 2 means mean \(\tfrac12\). If you typed 2, you read the rate as the mean.

When the average doesn't exist (Example 2.2.4). The Cauchy pdf \(\tfrac1\pi\cdot\tfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\) integrates to 1, but its tails fall off like \(1/x^2\), so \(x f(x)\) falls off only like \(1/x\), and \(\int^\infty \tfrac{dx}{x}\) diverges. Line by line: \(\mathrm E\lvert X\rvert = \tfrac2\pi\int_0^\infty \tfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx\) [symmetry], and \(\int_0^M \tfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx = \tfrac12\log(1 + M^2) \to \infty\) [substitute \(u = 1 + x^2\)]. The definition asks for \(\mathrm E\lvert X\rvert < \infty\) because, without it, the positive and negative halves are both infinite and "\(\infty - \infty\)" has no value.

Each of these is a pdf (each integrates to 1). Which one has a mean, \(\mathrm E X\), that exists?

\(x\cdot\tfrac{2}{x^3} = \tfrac{2}{x^2}\), whose integral over \((1, \infty)\) is 2: the mean exists and equals 2. The others: \(x\cdot\tfrac{1}{x^2} = \tfrac1x\) and \(x\cdot\tfrac12 x^{-3/2} = \tfrac12 x^{-1/2}\) both have divergent integrals, and the Cauchy's \(\mathrm E\lvert X\rvert = \infty\) (Example 2.2.4). A density can integrate to 1 while \(x f(x)\) does not: what decides it is how fast the tail thins out.

2. Average \(g(X)\) without finding the distribution of \(g(X)\) (from the reading, about 8 minutes)

Example 2.2.7, both ways, every line. \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\); find \(\mathrm E(-\log X)\).

Way 1, equation (2.2.4): weight \(g(x)\) by \(f_X\).

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm E(-\log X) &= \int_0^1 (-\log x)\cdot 1\,dx && \text{[definition; } f_X = 1 \text{ on } (0, 1)\text{]}\\ &= \Bigl[x - x\log x\Bigr]_0^1 && \text{[antiderivative of } -\log x\text{; check by differentiating]}\\ &= (1 - 0) - \lim_{x \to 0^+}(x - x\log x) = 1 && \text{[}x\log x \to 0 \text{ as } x \to 0^+\text{]} \end{aligned} $$

Way 2, equation (2.2.5): find \(f_Y\) first, then average \(y\). Lesson 12 found that \(Y = -\log X\) has \(f_Y(y) = e^{-y}\), \(y > 0\): exponential with mean 1. So \(\mathrm E Y = 1\) by Example 2.2.2 with \(\lambda = 1\).

Same answer, very different work. Way 2 needed a whole transformation first. Way 1 needed one integral. When you only want an average, use Way 1. Exercise 2.21 proves they always agree for monotone \(g\); the general proof is beyond this course.

\(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 2x\) for \(0 < x < 1\). Find \(\mathrm E(1/X)\) without finding the distribution of \(1/X\).

\(\mathrm E(1/X) = \int_0^1 \tfrac1x\cdot 2x\,dx = \int_0^1 2\,dx = 2\). The pdf of \(1/X\) never appears.

\(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) and \(Y = -\tfrac13\log X\). Find \(\mathrm E Y\) both ways: (a) as \(\int_0^1 g(x) f_X(x)\,dx\); (b) from \(f_Y(y) = 3e^{-3y}\), \(y > 0\), the pdf of \(Y\) from the warm-up. Type the common answer (a fraction or a decimal to 3 places).

(a) \(\int_0^1 -\tfrac13\log x\,dx = \tfrac13\cdot 1 = \tfrac13\) [constant out; Example 2.2.7's integral]. (b) \(3e^{-3y}\) is \(\tfrac1\lambda e^{-y/\lambda}\) with \(\lambda = \tfrac13\), so \(\mathrm E Y = \tfrac13\). Same number: this time Way 1 even reused an integral you already had.

\(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\). A student finds \(\mathrm E X^2\). Which step is wrong?

  1. \(\mathrm E X = \int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac12\).
  2. Since \(g(x) = x^2\), \(\mathrm E X^2 = g(\mathrm E X) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = \tfrac14\).
  3. So the average of \(X^2\) is \(\tfrac14\).

The definition weights \(g(x)\) by \(f_X\): \(\mathrm E X^2 = \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \tfrac13\), not \(\tfrac14\). In general \(\mathrm E\,g(X) \ne g(\mathrm E X)\) unless \(g\) is linear (\(ax + b\)). The gap \(\tfrac13 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac1{12}\) is no accident: it's \(\mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2\), as the next section's equation shows (take \(b = 0\) there).

Linearity (Theorem 2.2.5(a)) is the one case where \(g\) passes through. \(\mathrm E(a\,g_1(X) + b\,g_2(X) + c) = a\,\mathrm E g_1(X) + b\,\mathrm E g_2(X) + c\), because the integral is additive, constants come out of it, and \(\int c\,f_X = c\). In particular \(\mathrm E(aX + b) = a\,\mathrm E X + b\). Parts (b)–(d) say the average respects order: if \(g_1 \ge g_2\) everywhere, then \(\mathrm E g_1(X) \ge \mathrm E g_2(X)\).

\(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 3x^2\) for \(0 < x < 1\), so \(\mathrm E X = \tfrac34\). What is \(\mathrm E(5 - 4X)\)?

\(\mathrm E(5 - 4X) = 5 - 4\,\mathrm E X = 5 - 3 = 2\) [Theorem 2.2.5(a)]. No integral needed.

3. The best constant guess (from the reading, about 12 minutes)

You must guess \(X\) with a single number \(b\), before seeing it, and you pay \((X - b)^2\). Which \(b\) makes the average payment \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2\) smallest? You can't minimize \((X - b)^2\) itself: that's done by \(b = X\), which you don't know yet.

The trick: add and subtract the suspect. Guess that \(\mathrm E X\) is special, and write \(X - b = (X - \mathrm E X) + (\mathrm E X - b)\).

Expand and average.

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm E(X - b)^2 &= \mathrm E\bigl[(X - \mathrm E X) + (\mathrm E X - b)\bigr]^2\\ &= \mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2 + (\mathrm E X - b)^2 + 2\,\mathrm E\bigl[(X - \mathrm E X)(\mathrm E X - b)\bigr] && \text{[expand; linearity]} \end{aligned} $$

The second term needs no expectation: \(\mathrm E X - b\) is a constant.

The cross term is zero. \(\mathrm E\bigl[(X - \mathrm E X)(\mathrm E X - b)\bigr] = (\mathrm E X - b)\,\mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)\) [constant out] \(= (\mathrm E X - b)(\mathrm E X - \mathrm E X) = 0\) [linearity]. So, equation (2.2.2):

$$ \mathrm E(X - b)^2 = \mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2 + (\mathrm E X - b)^2 . $$

Read off the minimum. The first term doesn't involve \(b\). The second is a square, so it's \(\ge 0\), and it's 0 exactly when \(b = \mathrm E X\). So \(\min_b \mathrm E(X - b)^2 = \mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2\) (2.2.3), and the minimum is reached only at \(b = \mathrm E X\). That minimum, the average squared distance from the mean, is the variance (named in §2.3).

Where you've seen this (beyond the reading). A model trained on squared-error loss with no features at all learns to predict the mean of the training targets: that's this example with \(X\) a target picked at random from the training set. Swap squared error for absolute error, \(\mathrm E\lvert X - b\rvert\), and the best \(b\) becomes the median instead (C&B Exercise 2.18).

\(X\) has pdf \(f(x) = 3x^2\) for \(0 < x < 1\) (so \(\mathrm E X = \tfrac34\) and \(\mathrm E X^2 = \tfrac35\)). What is the smallest possible value of \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2\) over all constants \(b\)? (A fraction or a decimal to 4 places.)

At \(b = \tfrac34\): \(\mathrm E(X - \tfrac34)^2 = \mathrm E X^2 - 2\cdot\tfrac34\,\mathrm E X + \tfrac9{16} = \tfrac35 - \tfrac98 + \tfrac9{16} = \tfrac3{80} = 0.0375\).

Same \(X\) (pdf \(3x^2\) on \((0, 1)\), \(\mathrm E X = \tfrac34\), minimum of \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2\) equal to \(\tfrac3{80}\)). Someone guesses \(b = 1\) instead. Use equation (2.2.2), \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2 = \mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2 + (\mathrm E X - b)^2\), to find \(\mathrm E(X - 1)^2\) without a new integral. (A fraction or a decimal to 4 places.)

\(\tfrac3{80} + \left(\tfrac34 - 1\right)^2 = \tfrac3{80} + \tfrac1{16} = \tfrac8{80} = 0.1\). The penalty for guessing off the mean is exactly the squared miss, \((\mathrm E X - b)^2\).

Your proof, a second route. Adapted from Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.19. Let \(X\) have \(\mathrm E X^2 < \infty\) (this makes \(\mathrm E X\) and \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2\) finite, so \(h(b)\) is defined for every \(b\)), and let \(h(b) = \mathrm E(X - b)^2\). Using linearity first, write \(h(b)\) as a quadratic in \(b\). Then use calculus to show that \(h\) has its minimum at \(b = \mathrm E X\). Bracket a reason on the lines that use a fact about expectations or about minimizing.

h(b) = E(X² − 2bX + b²) = EX² − 2b EX + b² [linearity; b constant]; h'(b) = −2EX + 2b [differentiate a polynomial in b; no derivative under the integral needed], so h'(b) = 0 ⟺ b = EX; h''(b) = 2 > 0 (or: an upward parabola), so it's a minimum. Got it: the expansion via linearity, the critical point, and a reason it's a minimum (second derivative or parabola shape). Routine algebra needs no reason. Can't tell: right chain, no reason it's a minimum. Not yet: differentiating (X − b)² without averaging and treating X as b-dependent, or a false step.

\(h(b) = \mathrm E X^2 - 2b\,\mathrm E X + b^2\) [linearity]. \(h'(b) = 2b - 2\,\mathrm E X = 0 \iff b = \mathrm E X\), and \(h''(b) = 2 > 0\) [upward parabola], so \(b = \mathrm E X\) is the minimum. Expanding first is what made this easy: the book's version differentiates the integral directly, which needs the conditions in §2.4.

Go deeper: the binomial mean (Example 2.2.3), every line

From the reading (p. 56). \(X \sim\) binomial\((n, p)\): \(P(X = x) = \binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\), \(x = 0, \dots, n\).

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm E X &= \sum_{x=0}^{n} x\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x} = \sum_{x=1}^{n} x\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x} && \text{[the } x = 0 \text{ term is 0]}\\ &= \sum_{x=1}^{n} n\binom{n-1}{x-1} p^x(1-p)^{n-x} && \text{[}x\tbinom nx = n\tbinom{n-1}{x-1}\text{: choose a team of } x \text{ and its captain, two ways]}\\ &= np\sum_{y=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{y} p^{y}(1-p)^{n-1-y} && \text{[}y = x - 1\text{; pull out } np\text{]}\\ &= np && \text{[the sum is the total of the binomial}(n-1, p)\text{ pmf, which is 1]} \end{aligned} $$

The last move is the useful habit: when a sum or integral looks like a pmf or pdf you know, its total is 1.

Wrap-up

  • \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\) is \(g(x)\) averaged against the distribution of \(X\): \(\int g f_X\) or \(\sum g(x)P(X = x)\). No need for the distribution of \(g(X)\).
  • It exists only if \(\mathrm E\lvert g(X)\rvert < \infty\). The Cauchy, and \(1/x^2\) on \((1, \infty)\), have no mean.
  • Linearity: \(\mathrm E(aX + b) = a\,\mathrm E X + b\). For nonlinear \(g\), \(\mathrm E\,g(X) \ne g(\mathrm E X)\) in general.
  • \(\mathrm E(X - b)^2 = \mathrm E(X - \mathrm E X)^2 + (\mathrm E X - b)^2\): the mean is the best constant guess under squared error.

Extra practice (optional)

Problems from Casella & Berger, Chapter 2 exercises (pp. 77–78), easiest first. Answers are in the Casella & Berger solutions manual.

  1. Exercise 2.20: a couple has children until a daughter is born. Expected number of children? (Uses Example 1.5.4.)
  2. Exercise 2.11(a): \(\mathrm E X^2\) for a standard normal, directly and then via the pdf of \(Y = X^2\). The two ways from Part 2.
  3. Exercise 2.14(a): for nonnegative continuous \(X\), \(\mathrm E X = \int_0^\infty [1 - F_X(x)]\,dx\). (Hint: write \(x = \int_0^x dt\) and swap the order of integration.)
  4. Exercise 2.18: the median minimizes \(\mathrm E\lvert X - a\rvert\). The absolute-error partner of Part 3.

Extra reading: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., §4.5 "Law of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS)", and Example 4.3.14, the St. Petersburg paradox. The same definition, presented as a theorem, with the warning that \(\mathrm E\,g(X)\) is not \(g(\mathrm E X)\).

Extra article: Martin Peterson, "The St. Petersburg Paradox", Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2019, revised 2023), plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-stpetersburg. A coin-flipping game whose expected payout is infinite, though nobody would pay much to play it. It's the 1713 puzzle behind "expected value isn't the whole story", and the reason Daniel Bernoulli invented expected utility: exactly the \(\mathrm E\,g(X) \ne g(\mathrm E X)\) gap from Part 2.
